source.title: Double descent: When do neural quantum states generalize?
source.authors: M. Moss; Alev Orfi; Christopher Roth; Anirvan M. Sengupta; Antoine Georges; Dries Sels; Anna Dawid; A. Valenti

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether double descent appears in neural quantum states, a new setting, using supervised wavefunction-amplitude fitting and held-out test loss.
record.gate_note: The study sweeps network size and reports test-loss curves for several datasets and TFIM settings. It does not sweep training epochs. Although it varies the training-set size and discusses how the first test-loss minimum shifts, it does not directly test whether adding data near the interpolation threshold raises test error. Values in the plotted curves are not stated numerically. Infidelity is a distinct whole-state accuracy measure, not the held-out test loss; its results are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps network width in supervised neural quantum states (fully connected NNs fit to exact TFIM ground-state amplitudes) and reports held-out test loss. This is a new-setting test of model-wise double descent (V1) in deep networks. It has no epoch-wise, sample-wise, noise or regularization manipulations.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also say the peak's origin differs with training-data structure. Its location is consistently beyond the Hilbert-space dimension (Nparams > 2^N) in all settings, so practical NQS are underparameterized in this supervised setup.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses exact ground-state amplitudes as supervised labels, a Hellinger-inspired loss, and fully connected NQS on TFIM ground states; this differs from ordinary machine-learning prediction settings. The authors distinguish this setup from variational NQS training.
record.method_sensitivity: The curves vary with training-data composition and size, TFIM phase, and system size. Uniformly sampled datasets containing both high-probability configurations generalize better than those containing only one. The apparent peak and its location also vary across settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Variance of test loss and infidelity across ten seeds peaks near the interpolation threshold and then falls; training-loss variance falls monotonically.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Seed-to-seed variability of generalization peaks at the interpolation threshold (rugged test-loss landscape).

fits_no_version.finding: NQS trained on the full Hilbert space (no held-out set) show no double descent in infidelity (Fig. 15). The authors infer the test-loss peak is not an expressivity effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The double-descent peak arises from generalization to unseen configurations, not from non-monotone expressivity.

fits_no_version.finding: In the underparameterized regime, the first test-loss minimum sits near Nparams equal to the number of unique training configurations; this holds for top-X% and importance-sampled data but not uniform splits.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The optimal underparameterized size scales with the number of unique training samples.

record.problems: The experiments use a supervised setup with exact labels for a simple, exactly solvable TFIM, and the authors caution that typical variational NQS training may differ. The main size-sweep values are presented in plots rather than stated numerically. The second descent is not visible in the tested ferromagnetic size range.
record.rows_left_out: Infidelity-versus-size curves are not entered as rows because infidelity is a distinct whole-state accuracy metric rather than held-out test loss; the paper reports that it broadly follows the test-loss behavior. Other physical diagnostics, including normalization, parity, and correlation errors, are not test-loss results for the listed versions.

untested.parts: Only fully connected NQS on 1D TFIM ground states with supervised exact-amplitude labels and N=12/16; the variational NQS setting and standard ML tasks are not tested.
Training-set fraction varies (top 75/50/25%), but the test set changes with it, and no comparison shows more data raising test error at fixed size.
Only neural networks are used; no other model classes are studied.
No effective-complexity measure is proposed or tested across axes.
No label noise or regularization sweep, and no test for multiple peaks; the variance peak is descriptive only.

record.verdict_notes: V4 links were removed because NQS are deep feed-forward networks; extending double descent to a physics application of neural networks is a V1 test in a new setting, not a new model class. All values are figure-only. The interpolation threshold is defined by the authors as the training-loss minimum. Wide networks (W>432) were trained with a different learning-rate schedule and only for the Fig. 1 and Fig. 6 experiments; other experiments are capped at W≤432, which limits the size range for r2, r3, r5–r9. The paper is not one of the original sources.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests model-size behavior only in its supervised neural-quantum-state setup, not across standard deep-learning tasks generally.
No test-error sweep over training epochs is reported.
Training-set sizes are varied, but the study does not directly report that adding samples near the interpolation threshold raises test error.
The study tests an NQS setting only; it does not establish the curve across multiple non-neural-network model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting the peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.
The study does not manipulate label noise or regularization, test peak splitting, or determine whether variance causes the mean test-loss peak.
The study does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters to test whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.
